journeyIntro: For new connections and early romance. Practise curiosity, honest signals and comfortable boundaries.

lessons.title: Start With Curiosity
lessons.summary: Get to know someone without performing.

steps.title: Interested beats interesting
steps.body: Early dates can feel like an audition. But people usually leave feeling closest to whoever was most curious about them, not most impressive.

steps.prompt: Your date mentions they’ve just taken up bouldering, which you’ve never tried. What keeps the conversation flowing?

options.text: Nod along as if you climb all the time.
options.why: Pretending gets awkward fast, and you miss the chance to learn something real about them.

options.text: Steer it back to your own sporty achievements.
options.why: It turns their moment into your highlight reel, and they’re likely to switch off.

options.text: “I’ve never tried it! What got you hooked?”
options.why: Being honest that it’s new to you, plus a real question, invites them to share what they love.

steps.prompt: Ask the follow-up.
steps.why: Asking what lights them up gets you the good stories, and shows you want to know them.

steps.prompt: On a first date, what do you tend to do when you’re nervous?
steps.reply: Nerves are normal. One curious follow-up question is often all it takes to settle in.

steps.prompt: Opens the chat up or closes it down?

cards.text: “What’s the best part of your week usually?”
Turning every topic back to yourself

steps.why: Open questions and real interest give them room to share; short replies and self-focus leave nowhere to go.

steps.body: On your next date or chat, ask at least two follow-up questions about something they mention, before sharing your own story.

lessons.title: First Messages
lessons.summary: Open with something real, not just “hey”.

steps.title: Make the first message easy to answer
steps.body: “Hey” puts all the work on them. A message that mentions something from their profile shows you actually looked, and gives them something fun to reply to.

steps.prompt: Their profile mentions they just got back from hiking in Scotland. Which first message works best?

options.text: “Hey.”
options.why: Friendly, but it gives them nothing to work with.

options.text: “Scotland hiking! What was the best view, and did the midges win?”
options.why: Specific, playful and easy to answer, which starts a real chat.

options.text: “You’re gorgeous.”
options.why: A compliment on looks alone can feel generic, and doesn’t start a conversation.

steps.prompt: Ask about their world.
steps.before: I saw you’re into pottery. What got you
steps.why: Asking how they got into something invites a story, not a one-word reply.

steps.prompt: What do you find hardest about first messages?
steps.reply: A specific question about their profile solves most of these at once.

steps.prompt: Great opener, or conversation killer?

cards.text: “Best taco spot in town? I need your expert view 🌮”
“Your dog looks like trouble. What’s their name?”

steps.why: Great openers are light, specific and about them. Killers are vague, or make the other person do all the work.

steps.body: Next time you message a match, mention one specific thing from their profile and ask about it.

lessons.title: Beat First-Date Nerves
lessons.summary: Nerves are normal, and you can work with them.

steps.title: They’re probably nervous too
steps.body: Almost everyone feels nervous before a first date. A familiar place, a simple plan and a few questions in your back pocket make it much easier to relax and be yourself.

steps.prompt: You’re very nervous about a first date tomorrow. What helps most?

options.text: Plan a short coffee somewhere you know, and think of a few questions.
options.why: Familiar, short and low-pressure, so you can relax and enjoy it.

options.text: Book a fancy three-course dinner to impress them.
options.why: A long, formal date can add pressure if you don’t click.

options.text: Cancel. You’ll feel more ready another time.
options.why: Nerves rarely vanish by waiting, and you might miss someone great.

steps.prompt: It’s okay to name it.
steps.before: I’ll be honest, I’m a bit
steps.why: Admitting nerves lightly often breaks the ice, and they may feel the same.

steps.prompt: What helps you feel calmer before something new?
steps.reply: Use that before your next date. Being calm helps the real you come through.

steps.prompt: Getting ready for a first date. Put these in order.
items: Tell a friend where you’ll be
steps.why: A safe, familiar setting and a little preparation leave you free to relax and actually enjoy meeting them.

steps.body: Before your next first date, write down three questions you’d genuinely like to ask them.

lessons.title: Listen Beyond Words
lessons.summary: Show interest without rushing ahead.

steps.title: Listening is attractive
steps.body: Feeling truly listened to is rare, so it stands out. Put your phone away, follow their thread and resist jumping in with your own version.

steps.prompt: Your date tells you, a little embarrassed, about a disastrous first day at a new job. What’s the best response?

options.text: Jump in with an even more disastrous story of your own.
options.why: Topping their story can feel like competition, especially when they’ve just been vulnerable.

options.text: “Oh no, that sounds mortifying. What happened next?”
options.why: It names how it felt and keeps the spotlight on them, which makes it easier to open up.

options.text: “Honestly, you’re overthinking it.”
options.why: Even if kindly meant, it dismisses the feeling they just trusted you with.

steps.title: Your story can wait
steps.body: Sharing similar experiences builds connection, but timing matters. Let them finish, show you got it, then offer yours if it fits.

steps.prompt: Name the feeling first.
steps.after: . How did you get through it?
steps.why: Naming the feeling shows you were listening to how it felt, not just what happened.

steps.prompt: What pulls your attention away most on dates?
steps.reply: Knowing what distracts you is half the battle. Gently bring your focus back when you notice it.

steps.prompt: Listening or waiting to talk?

cards.text: Asking a follow-up about what they just said
“That’s nothing, listen to what happened to me…”
Putting your phone away when they speak
Nodding while rehearsing your next story

steps.why: Real listening shows in follow-up questions and remembered details, not just in staying quiet.

steps.body: Next time someone you’re dating shares a story, reflect one feeling you hear before telling a story of your own.

lessons.title: Read the Room
lessons.summary: Notice how they’re feeling, not just what they say.

steps.title: Listen with your eyes too
steps.body: A date tells you a lot without words: leaning in, laughing easily, or glancing at the door and giving short answers. Noticing these helps you adjust and keep them comfortable.

steps.prompt: Your date goes quiet and tense when you ask about their family. What’s the best move?

options.text: Ask more, you want to get to know them.
options.why: Pushing on a sore spot can make them feel uncomfortable.

options.text: Ask why they went quiet.
options.why: Kindly meant, but it can put them on the spot.

options.text: Lightly move on: “Anyway, tell me about that trip you mentioned!”
options.why: You respect their comfort and keep the date relaxed.

steps.prompt: Watch for comfort.
steps.why: Relaxed body language is a good sign the conversation is working.

steps.prompt: Which signal do you tend to miss?
steps.reply: Just noticing more makes you a much better date to be around.

steps.prompt: Enjoying it, or not so comfortable?

cards.text: Asking you lots of questions back

steps.why: Body language and energy say a lot. Noticing them helps you slow down, change topic or relax into it.

steps.body: On your next date, notice one moment when their energy changes, and gently adjust.

lessons.title: Make Space for Them
lessons.summary: Good dates feel balanced, not like a one-person show.

steps.title: Balance the conversation
steps.body: Nerves make some people talk non-stop and others go quiet. A great date feels like a game of catch: you share a bit, they share a bit, and you both ask questions.

steps.prompt: You realise you’ve been talking about your job for ten minutes. What now?

options.text: Keep going. They’re nodding, so it must be interesting.
options.why: Nodding can be politeness. They may want a turn.

options.text: “I’ve been chatting away! What about you, what keeps you busy?”
options.why: You notice the imbalance and warmly hand the conversation over.

options.text: Stop talking and wait for them to fill the gap.
options.why: Silence without an invitation can feel awkward.

steps.prompt: Pass the ball.
steps.why: A simple hand-over shows you’re as interested in them as in being heard.

steps.prompt: On dates, you tend to…
steps.reply: Knowing your habit helps you aim for that easy back-and-forth.

steps.title: A quiet date

lines.text: So yeah, that’s basically my whole week!

steps.prompt: They’ve said very little so far. What do you say?

options.text: Anyway, the other funny thing at work was…
options.why: Keeping the spotlight on you leaves them out of the conversation.

options.text: Enough about me! What’s been the best part of your week?
options.reaction: Oh! Actually, I adopted a cat 🐱
options.why: A warm, open question invites them in and evens things out.

options.text: You’re quiet. Are you having a bad time?
options.why: Pointing out their quietness can make them self-conscious.

steps.body: On your next date, notice who’s talking more, and hand the conversation over with a question.

lessons.title: Keep Your Own Pace
lessons.summary: You can enjoy dating without rushing.

steps.title: Excitement isn’t urgency
steps.body: When someone’s keen it’s tempting to say yes to everything. But a pace that suits you makes dating more enjoyable, and shows what each of you is like.

steps.prompt: After a great date, they ask to meet again tomorrow. You like them but need a quiet night. What do you say?

options.text: “I’d love to! Tomorrow’s tricky, but how about Saturday?”
options.why: It shows clear interest and offers a real alternative, so your “not tomorrow” isn’t a “no”.

options.text: Say yes, then spend the evening tired and flat.
options.why: You won’t be at your best, and they get a less true picture of who you are.

options.text: Leave the message unanswered until you feel like replying.
options.why: Silence after a good date can feel like rejection and leave them anxious and guessing.

steps.prompt: Offer an alternative.
steps.why: A specific alternative makes your interest obvious and keeps the plan moving.

steps.prompt: What pace feels right for you early on?
options: A couple of times a week
steps.reply: Any of those is fine. What matters is noticing your pace and saying it out loud.

steps.title: A big invitation

lines.text: So my family’s having a barbecue on Sunday…
Want to come and meet everyone? 😊

steps.prompt: It’s only date three and it feels fast. Reply:

options.text: Sure, sounds fun!
options.reaction: Amazing! My mum will love you 😄
options.why: Saying yes when you’re uneasy sets a pace that doesn’t feel right for you.

options.text: Haha, maybe!
options.why: A vague answer leaves them guessing and puts off the honest bit.

options.text: That’s really sweet. It feels a bit soon for me, but I’d love to see you on Saturday?
options.why: You’re warm, honest about your pace and offer another way to meet, so nobody feels rejected.

steps.body: Next time a plan doesn’t suit you, say what does work instead, with a specific day or time.

lessons.title: Date Safely
lessons.summary: Small safety habits let you relax and enjoy it.

steps.title: Safety and fun go together
steps.body: Meeting somewhere public, getting there on your own and telling a friend your plans aren’t signs of distrust. They’re simple habits that let you relax and enjoy getting to know someone.

steps.prompt: Your match suggests picking you up from home for your first date. What’s the safest response?

options.text: Give them your address. It’s a kind offer.
options.why: Probably meant kindly, but it’s wise to keep your address private at first.

options.text: “Thanks! I’ll meet you there, it’s easier for me.”
options.why: Friendly and firm, and you keep control of getting home.

options.text: Cancel. It feels like a red flag.
options.why: It may just be kindness. A simple no thank you is enough.

steps.prompt: A simple safety habit.
steps.after: with a friend during the date.
steps.why: Letting a friend know where you are is a quick, easy safety net.

steps.prompt: Which safety habit do you already use?
steps.reply: Adding one more habit makes future dates feel safer and more relaxed.

steps.prompt: Safe habit, or worth rethinking?

cards.text: Going back to theirs on the first date
Telling a friend where you’ll be
Letting them drive you home the first time

steps.why: Safe habits keep you in control. They’re not about suspicion, just looking after yourself while you get to know someone.

steps.body: Before your next first date, tell a friend where you’ll be and plan how you’ll get home.

lessons.title: Keep Your Life Full
lessons.summary: Don’t drop friends and hobbies for someone new.

steps.title: Don’t disappear into dating
steps.body: When someone new is exciting, it’s tempting to cancel friends and skip your hobbies. Keeping your own life full makes you happier and more yourself, which is attractive too.

steps.prompt: Your new date asks to meet on the night of your weekly five-a-side football. What’s best?

options.text: Skip football. This is more important.
options.why: One night is fine, but making a habit of it slowly shrinks your life.

options.text: Tell them you’re busy, without saying why.
options.why: Being vague can feel like a brush-off.

options.text: “That’s my football night! How about Thursday instead?”
options.why: You keep what matters to you and still show you want to see them.

steps.prompt: Protect what matters.
steps.why: Sharing your plans shows you have a full life, and gives them an easy alternative.

steps.prompt: What do you most want to keep up while dating?
steps.reply: Holding onto it helps you stay grounded, however exciting things get.

steps.prompt: Match each habit with a healthy way to keep it.

pairs.b: Keep the date in your diary

steps.why: A healthy relationship fits around your life, rather than replacing it.

steps.body: This week, keep one plan with a friend or hobby, even if a date is on offer.

lessons.title: Notice the Small Signs
lessons.summary: Build connection through thoughtful attention.

steps.title: Remembering is romantic
steps.body: Asking how their sister’s wedding went, or remembering how they take their coffee, quietly says, “I was paying attention to you.”

steps.prompt: On your second date, they mention a big job interview next Thursday. What builds connection?

options.text: Text several times on the day asking for updates.
options.why: Caring, but on a stressful day lots of messages can feel like pressure early on.

options.text: Say nothing; they’ll mention it if it matters.
options.why: They may read the silence as you not having listened, even if you did.

options.text: Wish them luck, then ask how it went after Thursday.
options.why: Following up shows you remembered what mattered to them, without crowding them.

steps.prompt: Follow up on a detail.
steps.before: Good luck on Thursday! I’d love to
steps.why: It shows you care about the outcome while leaving them space to share when they’re ready.

steps.prompt: How do you usually show interest early in dating?
steps.reply: All good signs. Remembering small details is one of the quietest and most powerful.

steps.prompt: Match each detail they shared with a thoughtful follow-up.
steps.why: Following up on small things shows you were really listening, and that’s what makes someone feel seen.

steps.body: Follow up on one detail someone you’re dating mentioned last time: an event, a worry or a plan.

lessons.title: Texting Between Dates
lessons.summary: Keep the spark going without overthinking.

steps.title: Between dates, keep it light
steps.body: Texts between dates are about staying in touch, not having deep talks or analysing every reply. A quick “that reminded me of you” goes further than a long essay.

steps.prompt: You had a great second date yesterday. What’s a good message today?

options.text: Wait three days so you don’t seem keen.
options.why: Playing games can make them think you’re not interested.

options.text: A long message analysing how the date went.
options.why: Lovely intent, but it can feel heavy this early.

options.text: “Had a really fun time last night. That dessert is still on my mind 😄”
options.why: Warm, light and honest, and it gives them an easy reply.

steps.prompt: A light check-in.
steps.why: Small, playful messages keep the connection going between dates.

steps.prompt: What’s your texting worry?
steps.reply: Most people care far less about timing than you think. Warmth matters more.

steps.prompt: Keeps the spark going, or overdoing it?

cards.text: A funny photo that reminded you of them
Ten messages in a row with no reply
Asking where they are all the time

steps.why: Light, caring messages build connection. Too many, or too much checking up, can feel like pressure.

steps.body: Send one light, warm message to someone you’re dating, without overthinking it.

lessons.title: Plan Thoughtful Dates
lessons.summary: Dates built around them say “I listened”.

steps.title: A date that fits them
steps.body: Remembering they love Thai food, or that they wanted to try climbing, and planning around it shows you were paying attention. It doesn’t need to be expensive.

steps.prompt: On your last date, they mentioned they’d always wanted to try paddleboarding. What’s a thoughtful next date?

options.text: Dinner at your favourite restaurant.
options.why: Nice, but it doesn’t show you remembered what they said.

options.text: “Fancy finally trying paddleboarding? I found a beginner session Saturday.”
options.why: It shows you listened and turns their wish into a shared adventure.

options.text: Let them pick everything from now on.
options.why: Generous, but planning something for them shows care.

steps.prompt: Use what you remember.
steps.after: , so I booked the noodle bar!
steps.why: Bringing back a detail they shared makes the date feel personal.

steps.prompt: What kind of date do you enjoy planning most?
steps.reply: Mixing your style with what they love is the sweet spot.

steps.prompt: Match each detail they shared with a date idea.

pairs.b: Tickets to a small local gig

steps.why: Turning a small detail into a plan is one of the clearest ways to show you care.

steps.body: Plan your next date around something they’ve mentioned they’d love to do.

lessons.title: Trust Takes Time
lessons.summary: Let actions and words line up gradually.

steps.title: Words are a start
steps.body: Early on, it’s easy to fall for lovely words and big plans. Trust is built when what someone says and what they do line up, again and again.

steps.prompt: After two dates, they talk about taking you to Paris this summer. What’s the healthiest way to take it?

options.text: Enjoy the sweetness, and watch whether their everyday actions match.
options.why: You can feel flattered and still let trust grow from consistency, not grand promises.

options.text: Take it as proof they’re serious about you.
options.why: Big promises this early are easy to make; they don’t yet show how someone will treat you.

options.text: Set them a little test to see if they mean it.
options.why: Tests tend to backfire and start the relationship on suspicion instead of honesty.

steps.title: What consistency looks like
steps.body: Turning up on time, replying in a steady way, doing what they said. Small, boring reliability tells you far more than an exciting promise.

steps.prompt: Finish the thought.
steps.why: Actions over time are the most reliable guide to how someone will treat you.

steps.prompt: Green flag, or one to watch?

cards.text: Does what they said they’d do
Says “I love you” on the second date
Gets sulky when you see your friends

steps.why: Trust is built on steady, respectful actions over time; intense promises or possessiveness early on are worth watching.

steps.body: This week, notice one small action from someone you’re dating that matches (or doesn’t match) what they’ve said.

lessons.title: Show Up as Promised
lessons.summary: Reliability early on shows who you really are.

steps.title: Early dates are a preview
steps.body: When you’re getting to know someone, every small action is a clue. Arriving on time, replying when you said you would and not cancelling last minute show you can be counted on.

steps.prompt: You’ve got a date tonight, but friends just invited you to something more fun. What builds trust?

options.text: Cancel the date with a vague excuse.
options.why: Last-minute cancelling early on can make them feel unimportant.

options.text: Go on the date as planned.
options.why: Keeping your word, even when tempted, shows you’re reliable.

options.text: Go to both and leave the date early.
options.why: Being half there can feel worse than not showing up.

steps.prompt: If you must cancel.
steps.before: I’m so sorry to cancel. Can we
steps.why: Offering a new time straight away shows you still want to see them.

steps.prompt: What makes you trust someone you’re dating?
steps.reply: Showing those same things yourself helps trust grow both ways.

steps.prompt: Reliable, or a bit flaky?

cards.text: Arriving when you said you would
Letting them know if you’re running late

steps.why: Reliability early on is how someone learns they can trust you with more later.

steps.body: Keep every small promise to the person you’re dating this week, even the tiny ones.

lessons.title: Open Up Gradually
lessons.summary: Share a little more as trust grows.

steps.title: Trust grows step by step
steps.body: Sharing everything on a first date can feel like too much, but never opening up keeps things shallow. Sharing a little more each time, and seeing how it’s received, builds trust safely.

steps.prompt: It’s your second date, and they ask why your last relationship ended. It was painful. What’s healthiest?

options.text: Share every detail. Honesty is everything.
options.why: Honesty matters, but you don’t owe the full story this early.

options.text: Refuse to talk about it at all.
options.why: A flat no can feel like a wall. A short answer is kinder.

options.text: “We wanted different things. Happy to share more as we get to know each other.”
options.why: Honest and kind, while keeping the deeper details for when trust has grown.

steps.prompt: Share at your pace.
steps.before: I’d like to tell you more about that when we know each other
steps.why: It shows openness while protecting what’s still tender.

steps.prompt: How quickly do you usually open up?
steps.reply: Noticing your pace helps you share in a way that feels safe for you.

steps.prompt: Opening up over time. Put these in order.
steps.why: Opening up in layers lets trust build. You see how each share is received before going deeper.

steps.body: On your next date, share one thing a little more personal than usual, and notice how it’s received.

lessons.title: Talking About Exes
lessons.summary: Keep the past short, fair and kind.

steps.title: How you talk about exes says a lot
steps.body: A date will learn more from how you describe your exes than from the details. Being fair and brief, even about a painful break-up, shows maturity and kindness.

steps.prompt: Your date asks about your ex. They cheated on you. What’s the best way to answer?

options.text: Spend twenty minutes on how awful they were.
options.why: Understandable, but it can make the date feel heavy and stuck in the past.

options.text: “It ended badly, and I learnt a lot. I’m in a much better place now.”
options.why: Honest and brief, and it shows you’ve moved forward.

options.text: Pretend you’ve never had a serious relationship.
options.why: A small fib can cause bigger trust problems later.

steps.prompt: Keep it short and fair.
steps.before: We weren’t right for each other, and I
steps.why: Focusing on what you learnt keeps it positive and shows growth.

steps.prompt: How do you feel talking about your past relationships?
steps.reply: All normal. You can always say “I’ll share more when we know each other better.”

steps.prompt: Match each bitter line with a fairer one.

pairs.b: “It was hard, but I’ve moved on.”

steps.why: Fair, short answers show you can handle hard things gracefully, which builds trust.

steps.body: Practise a short, fair one-line answer about your last relationship for the next time it comes up.

lessons.title: Talk About Mixed Signals
lessons.summary: Ask instead of decoding every message.

steps.title: Stop decoding, start asking
steps.body: Reading meaning into reply times and emoji is exhausting, and often wrong. One kind, direct question usually saves days of guessing.

steps.prompt: Their messages are warm, but they never suggest meeting up. You’re not sure where you stand. What do you do?

options.text: Drop hints about free evenings and hope they notice.
options.why: Hints are easy to miss, and you’ll end up decoding their silence all over again.

options.text: “I really enjoy chatting. Would you like to meet up again?”
options.why: It’s friendly, clear and easy to answer, so you get real information instead of guesses.

options.text: Decide they’re playing games and go cold.
options.why: They might just be shy or busy; going cold can end something good on a guess.

steps.prompt: Make the question clear.
steps.why: A specific, light invitation is easy to say yes or no to, and either answer helps you.

steps.prompt: When signals are mixed, what do you usually do?
steps.reply: It’s natural to want certainty. A short, kind question is often the quickest route to it.

steps.title: Back after a silence

lines.text: Sorry I went quiet, work’s been mad this week 😩

steps.prompt: It’s been four days. What do you say?

options.text: Oh, I hadn’t even noticed 🙂
options.why: Playing it cool hides what you feel, so nothing gets clearer.

options.text: Good to hear from you! I’ll be honest, the silence left me unsure. I like regular chats.
options.reaction: Fair point. I’ll be better at saying when I’m busy 😊
options.why: You’re warm and honest about what you need, which helps you both see if you’re a match.

options.text: Four days. Really?
options.why: Leading with blame makes them defensive before you’ve said what you want.

steps.body: Next time you catch yourself decoding a message, ask one clear, friendly question instead.

lessons.title: Say That You Like Them
lessons.summary: Letting someone know you’re keen is brave and kind.

steps.title: Being clear is attractive
steps.body: Playing it cool can leave both people guessing. A simple, warm “I really like spending time with you” takes courage, and usually makes the other person feel great.

steps.prompt: You’ve had four lovely dates and you really like them. How do you let them know?

options.text: Act a bit distant so you don’t seem too keen.
options.why: They may read it as you losing interest.

options.text: “I really enjoy being with you. I’d love to keep seeing you.”
options.why: Honest and warm, without pressure, so they know where they stand.

options.text: Wait for them to say it first.
options.why: If you both wait, nobody says it.

steps.prompt: Say it simply.
steps.why: Simple, warm words are easier to say and to hear than big declarations.

steps.prompt: What stops you saying you like someone?
steps.reply: Those fears are normal. Being kind and clear is still worth it.

steps.title: After a lovely evening

lines.text: I had such a good time tonight 😊

steps.prompt: You really like them. Reply:

options.text: Cool, glad you got back okay.
options.why: Polite, but it hides how much you enjoyed it.

options.text: Me too! I really like spending time with you. Same time next week? 😊
options.reaction: Yes! I was hoping you’d say that 🥰
options.why: Warm and clear, so they know you’re keen and can feel the same.

options.text: Glad you’re home. Night.
options.why: Short replies after a great date can feel like a cool-off.

steps.body: Tell someone you’re dating one specific thing you enjoy about spending time with them.

lessons.title: End Things Kindly
lessons.summary: A short, kind goodbye beats ghosting.

steps.title: Ghosting leaves people guessing
steps.body: Going silent can feel easier, but it leaves the other person confused and hurt. A short, kind message lets them move on, and lets you leave with a clear conscience.

steps.prompt: After three dates, you don’t feel a spark. They’ve asked to meet again. What do you do?

options.text: Stop replying.
options.why: Ghosting leaves them wondering what went wrong.

options.text: Say yes and hope the spark arrives.
options.why: Going along with it can waste both your time.

options.text: “I’ve enjoyed meeting you, but I don’t feel a romantic spark. I wish you all the best.”
options.why: Honest, brief and kind, which is the most respectful way to end it.

steps.prompt: Keep it kind and clear.
steps.before: You’re great, but I don’t think we’re the right
steps.why: “Not the right match” is honest without criticising them.

steps.prompt: Have you ever been ghosted?
steps.reply: Remembering how it feels makes it easier to choose a kind goodbye.

steps.prompt: Kind ending, or unkind?

cards.text: Fading out slowly so they “get the hint”

steps.why: A kind ending is clear, brief and respectful. It ends the uncertainty without adding hurt.

steps.body: If you need to end something, send a short, kind message rather than going quiet.

lessons.title: Disagree With Respect
lessons.summary: Different opinions need not end connection.

steps.title: Differences are information
steps.body: Early disagreements are a preview of how you handle tension together. Kind curiosity, rather than winning, tells you whether you’re a good fit.

steps.prompt: You love lazy weekends; they like packing weekends with plans. It comes up on your fourth date. What’s the best response?

options.text: Tease them that they must be exhausting to live with.
options.why: Mocking a preference this early can sting and make them guarded with you.

options.text: “We’re pretty different there! What do you love about busy weekends?”
options.why: It names the difference lightly and gets curious, so you learn about each other.

options.text: Pretend you love busy weekends too.
options.why: Hiding who you are avoids tension now but builds a relationship on a version that isn’t you.

steps.title: Notice how they disagree
steps.body: Can you both differ without mocking, sulking or pressure? Respectful disagreement is a green flag; contempt or control is a red one.

steps.prompt: When you disagree with someone new, what do you tend to do?
steps.reply: Noticing your pattern helps you stay yourself while staying kind.

steps.prompt: You want different things. Put these in order.
items: Try a mix of the two
steps.why: Listening first lowers the guard; looking for shared goals turns a clash into a plan you can both enjoy.

steps.body: When you notice a difference with someone you’re dating, ask one curious question about their view before sharing yours.

lessons.title: Different Backgrounds
lessons.summary: Get curious about how they grew up.

steps.title: Differences can be interesting
steps.body: People bring their culture, faith and family habits into dating. Instead of seeing differences as problems, getting curious about them can bring you closer.

steps.prompt: Your date mentions their family expects them home for a big meal every Sunday, which feels unusual to you. What’s best?

options.text: “That sounds lovely. What’s Sunday like in your family?”
options.why: Curiosity shows respect and helps you understand what matters to them.

options.text: “That sounds a bit controlling.”
options.why: Judging their family early on can feel like an attack.

options.text: Say nothing, but quietly worry about it.
options.why: Unspoken worries tend to grow. A question is better.

steps.prompt: Ask with interest.
steps.why: Asking what something means invites a story instead of a defence.

steps.prompt: Which difference would you most want to understand in a partner?
steps.reply: Curious questions early on make big differences much easier to navigate later.

steps.prompt: Match each difference with a curious question.
steps.why: Curious questions turn differences into conversations, and help you see if your lives could fit together.

steps.body: Ask someone you’re dating about one tradition or value from how they grew up.

lessons.title: Your First Disagreement
lessons.summary: The first tiff shows how you’ll handle harder ones.

steps.title: First tiffs are a good test
steps.body: Every couple disagrees eventually. How you both handle the first small one, staying calm, listening and making up, is a great sign of how you’ll handle bigger things.

steps.prompt: Your date was annoyed you were 40 minutes late without texting. They’re a bit cold. What’s best?

options.text: “It’s only 40 minutes, don’t be dramatic.”
options.why: Dismissing their feelings turns a small issue into a bigger one.

options.text: Act like nothing happened.
options.why: Ignoring it leaves them feeling unheard.

options.text: “You’re right, I should have texted. I’m sorry. It won’t happen again.”
options.why: Owning it quickly and kindly shows you can be trusted to repair.

steps.prompt: Repair quickly.
steps.before: I’m sorry. I can see why that
steps.why: Acknowledging how it affected them makes the apology land.

steps.prompt: When there’s tension early on, you tend to…
steps.reply: Knowing your reaction helps you choose a calm, open response instead.

steps.title: A small clash

lines.text: I felt a bit embarrassed when you joked about my job in front of your friends.

steps.prompt: Reply:

options.text: You’re not being silly. I’m sorry I embarrassed you. I’ll be more thoughtful.
options.reaction: Thank you. That means a lot 😊
options.why: You validate their feeling and repair it, which builds trust fast.

options.text: It was just a joke, lighten up!
options.why: Brushing it off tells them their feelings don’t matter.

options.text: Well, you laughed at the time.
options.reaction: I didn’t want to make a scene…
options.why: Arguing about the details misses that they were hurt.

steps.body: If a small tension comes up with someone you’re dating, address it calmly the same day.

lessons.title: Handle a No Kindly
lessons.summary: Respect another person’s limits and your own.

steps.title: A no is trust, not rejection
steps.body: When someone tells you their limit, they’re trusting you with honesty. Responding warmly makes it safe for them to be honest again.

steps.prompt: At the end of a lovely evening, your date says they’d rather not kiss yet. What’s the best response?

options.text: Ask why not until they explain themselves.
options.why: Pushing for reasons turns a clear no into pressure, which is never okay.

options.text: “Of course, thanks for telling me. I had a great time tonight.”
options.why: It respects their pace without fuss and keeps the warmth of the evening intact.

options.text: Go quiet and sulk for the rest of the night.
options.why: Sulking punishes honesty, and they may feel they can’t tell you their limits again.

steps.title: Your no counts too
steps.body: The same goes the other way. You never owe anyone an explanation for a limit, and anyone worth dating will accept it without pushing.

steps.prompt: Respond to a boundary.
steps.why: Thanking them shows their honesty was welcome, which builds real trust between you.

steps.prompt: Is there a limit of your own you’d like to feel comfortable saying?
steps.placeholder: I’d like to be able to say…

steps.prompt: Respectful or pushy?

cards.text: Acting cold for the rest of the night
Keeping the evening warm and easy

steps.why: Accepting a no gracefully, without sulking or asking again, is what makes someone feel safe with you.

steps.body: Practise one warm response to a no, and one way to say your own, so both feel easy when the moment comes.

lessons.title: Check In as You Go
lessons.summary: Asking “is this okay?” is caring, not awkward.

steps.title: Consent is an ongoing chat
steps.body: Checking in, “Is this okay?” or “Want to slow down?”, isn’t a mood killer. It shows care and makes the other person feel safe to be honest, which brings you closer.

steps.prompt: Things are getting more physical, and your date seems a little hesitant. What’s the best move?

options.text: Keep going. They’d say if they weren’t okay.
options.why: Many people freeze or feel unable to speak up. It’s on both of you to check.

options.text: “Are you comfortable? We can slow down, no pressure at all.”
options.why: Checking in gently makes it easy for them to be honest.

options.text: Stop suddenly and go quiet.
options.why: Stopping is right, but silence can make them feel they did something wrong.

steps.prompt: A caring check-in.
steps.why: A simple question shows respect and keeps trust strong.

steps.prompt: How comfortable are you checking in with a partner?
steps.reply: It gets easier with practice, and most people really appreciate it.

steps.prompt: Respectful check-in, or pressure?

cards.text: Asking again after they said no

steps.why: Respect means a yes is freely given and a no is fully accepted. Checking in makes both easy to say.

steps.body: Practise one natural check-in phrase that feels like you, so it’s ready when you need it.

lessons.title: When You’re Turned Down
lessons.summary: Handle rejection with grace, and look after yourself.

steps.title: Rejection is part of dating
steps.body: Being turned down stings, but it’s a normal part of finding the right person. Replying graciously keeps your dignity, and treating yourself kindly afterwards helps you bounce back.

steps.prompt: After two dates, they message: “You’re lovely, but I don’t feel a spark.” What’s the best reply?

options.text: “Thanks for being honest. Best of luck!”
options.why: Gracious and brief, and you keep your dignity.

options.text: “Can you tell me what I did wrong?”
options.why: Understandable, but they may not have a clear answer.

options.text: “Your loss.”
options.why: It might feel good for a second, but it’s not kind to either of you.

steps.prompt: Be kind to yourself.
steps.before: It wasn’t the right match, and that doesn’t mean I’m not
steps.why: One person’s no is about fit, not about your worth.

steps.prompt: What helps you feel better after a rejection?
steps.reply: Plan a little of that the next time it stings.

steps.prompt: Bouncing back. Put these in order.
items: Reply kindly, or not at all
steps.why: A gracious reply, a little self-care and time to recover help you return to dating feeling stronger.

steps.body: Write a kind, short reply you could use if someone turns you down, so you’re not caught off guard.

lessons.title: Be Clear About Hopes
lessons.summary: Share intentions without demanding certainty.

steps.title: Honesty about what you want
steps.body: Hiding what you’re looking for to seem easy-going often leads to months of mismatched hopes. Saying it kindly saves you both time.

steps.prompt: You’ve been on several dates and you’d like something committed, but you’ve never discussed it. What do you do?

options.text: Share what you’re hoping for and ask what they’re looking for.
options.why: It’s honest without demanding an answer on the spot, and invites them to be honest too.

options.text: Assume you’re exclusive after this many dates.
options.why: People often have different assumptions; guessing can lead to real hurt later on.

options.text: Keep quiet so you don’t seem too keen.
options.why: Playing it cool can leave you invested in something that may want something else.

steps.title: Share, don’t demand
steps.body: “I’m enjoying this and I’m looking for something serious eventually. What about you?” It’s clear, calm and leaves room for their honest answer.

steps.prompt: Say what you hope for.
steps.before: I’m enjoying this, and I’m hoping for
steps.why: It’s honest about your hopes without pressure or erasing what you want.

steps.prompt: What are you hoping for from dating right now?

steps.title: The big question

lines.text: What are you actually looking for right now?

steps.prompt: You’d like something serious. Reply:

options.text: Honestly? Something serious, when it’s right. What about you?
options.reaction: Same, honestly. I’m glad you said it 😊
options.why: You’re clear about your hopes without pressure, and you invite them to be honest too.

options.text: Oh, I’m just seeing where things go!
options.why: Hiding what you want can lead you both down a path that doesn’t fit.

options.text: Why, what are YOU looking for?
options.why: Dodging the question makes it harder for either of you to be open.

steps.body: Write down what you’re looking for, then share it with someone you’re dating when the moment feels right.

lessons.title: The Exclusive Talk
lessons.summary: Ask where you stand, calmly and clearly.

steps.title: Don’t guess, ask
steps.body: After a few weeks, you might wonder whether you’re exclusive. Guessing creates anxiety. A calm, warm question, without an ultimatum, gets you clarity.

steps.prompt: You’ve been seeing someone for two months and want to know if you’re exclusive. What’s the best approach?

options.text: Check their dating app to see if they’re active.
options.why: Snooping creates distrust and doesn’t give you their answer.

options.text: “I really like where this is going. Are you seeing anyone else?”
options.why: Warm, direct and honest, so you get clarity without pressure.

options.text: Wait for them to bring it up.
options.why: You could be waiting a while, feeling unsure the whole time.

steps.prompt: Ask calmly.
steps.after: . How do you feel about that?
steps.why: Saying what you want, then asking how they feel, opens a real conversation.

steps.prompt: How do you feel about asking “what are we?”
steps.reply: It’s normal to feel nervous. Clarity is usually a relief, whatever the answer.

steps.title: The question

lines.text: Can I ask something? Are we seeing other people?
Honestly, I’m not seeing anyone else. But I hadn’t thought about labels yet.

steps.prompt: You’d like to be exclusive. Reply:

options.text: Okay, forget I asked!
options.why: Backing off hides what you want and leaves you still unsure.

options.text: If you’re not sure, maybe we should stop.
options.why: An ultimatum adds pressure before they’ve had time to think.

options.text: That’s fair! I’d love us to be exclusive. No rush, have a think and tell me how you feel.
options.reaction: I’d really like that too, actually 😊
options.why: You say what you want and give them space to answer honestly.

steps.body: If you’re unsure where you stand with someone, ask them calmly this week instead of guessing.

lessons.title: Meet Their People
lessons.summary: Meeting friends and family is a big, lovely step.

steps.title: Their people matter
steps.body: Meeting someone’s friends or family shows you’re becoming part of their life. Being curious, warm and yourself matters far more than making a perfect impression.

steps.prompt: You’re meeting your partner’s best friends for the first time. What helps most?

options.text: Ask your partner a bit about each friend beforehand.
options.why: It gives you easy things to talk about and shows you care.

options.text: Stay quiet so you don’t say the wrong thing.
options.why: Quiet can come across as uninterested.

options.text: Tell lots of stories to seem interesting.
options.why: Dominating the chat can make it harder for them to get to know you.

steps.prompt: Show interest in them.
steps.why: Showing you know a little about them makes friends feel welcomed.

steps.prompt: How do you feel about meeting a partner’s family?
steps.reply: Nerves are normal. Being curious and kind is all you need.

steps.prompt: Meeting their friends. Put these in order.
items: Arrive on time with a smile
steps.why: A little preparation and genuine interest make you easy to warm to.

steps.body: Before you next meet a partner’s friends or family, ask your partner one thing about each person.

lessons.title: The Big Values Talk
lessons.summary: Kids, money, faith: talk before it’s too late.

steps.title: Big values, early enough
steps.body: Do you want children? How do you feel about money, faith or where to live? These aren’t first-date topics, but as things get serious, talking about them helps you both choose wisely.

steps.prompt: You’ve been together six months and you really want children one day. You’ve never discussed it. What’s best?

options.text: Wait a couple of years. It might sort itself out.
options.why: If you want different things, waiting makes it harder to face.

options.text: Bring it up in the middle of an argument.
options.why: Big topics deserve a calm moment, not a heated one.

options.text: “Can we talk about the future? I’d love to know how you feel about kids one day.”
options.why: A calm, curious question helps you both see if your futures fit.

steps.prompt: Ask openly.
steps.why: Asking how they feel, not what they’ll do, keeps the talk open and safe.

steps.prompt: Which big value would you most need to talk about with a serious partner?
steps.placeholder: e.g. where we want to live

steps.prompt: Early-date topic, or a later, bigger talk?
steps.why: Light topics build connection early on. Big values deserve a calm talk once things are getting serious.

steps.body: If things are getting serious, suggest one calm conversation about a big future topic.

lessons.title: Choose What Feels Healthy
lessons.summary: Check whether this connection fits your values.

steps.title: Chemistry isn’t the whole story
steps.body: Butterflies are lovely, but they can’t tell you if a connection is good for you. How you feel around someone, over time, matters more.

steps.prompt: A new relationship feels exciting, but you sometimes feel rushed into things. What’s the healthiest next step?

options.text: Ignore it; the chemistry is too good to risk.
options.why: Strong chemistry can make it easy to overlook signs that matter for your wellbeing.

options.text: Let your friends decide whether to keep seeing them.
options.why: Friends can help you think it through, but your own feelings deserve to lead.

options.text: Notice the pressure, say what pace suits you and see how they respond.
options.why: How someone reacts to your limits shows you a lot about whether this is healthy for you.

steps.title: If something feels wrong
steps.body: Healthy relationships never involve fear, control or harm. If you ever feel unsafe or pressured, talk to someone you trust or a local support line.

steps.prompt: How do you usually feel after time with them?
steps.reply: Your feelings after time together are useful information. Keep listening to them.

steps.prompt: Match each feeling with a healthy next step.

pairs.b: Check the story in your head
Keep one night just for you

steps.why: Feelings are useful signals. Noticing them and acting on them keeps a new relationship healthy for you.

steps.body: After your next date, take a moment to notice how you feel: relaxed, anxious, energised or drained.

lessons.title: Healthy or Unhealthy?
lessons.summary: Know the signs of a relationship that’s good for you.

steps.title: Healthy love feels safe
steps.body: A healthy relationship feels mostly calm, respectful and fun. If you often feel anxious, controlled or like you’re walking on eggshells, that’s worth taking seriously.

steps.prompt: Your partner gets upset whenever you see friends without them, and checks your phone. What’s healthiest?

options.text: See friends less so they don’t get upset.
options.why: Shrinking your life to keep the peace is a warning sign.

options.text: Talk to a trusted friend about it, and take it seriously.
options.why: Controlling behaviour is a red flag. An outside view helps you see clearly.

options.text: It’s just because they love you so much.
options.why: Love doesn’t look like control. That story can keep people stuck.

steps.prompt: A healthy check.
steps.before: In a healthy relationship, I can still see my
steps.why: Keeping your friendships is a simple, important sign that a relationship is healthy.

steps.prompt: How do you usually feel around a partner?
steps.reply: Your feelings are useful information. If anxiety is constant, it’s worth talking to someone you trust.

steps.prompt: Healthy sign, or warning sign?
steps.why: Healthy love respects your freedom. Control, checking and isolating are warning signs, however loving they’re made to sound.

steps.body: Think about how you feel around the person you’re dating. If anything worries you, talk to someone you trust.

lessons.title: Grow Together
lessons.summary: Keep the closeness as the newness fades.

steps.title: After the honeymoon
steps.body: The early buzz naturally calms down. That’s not a bad sign. Couples who keep being curious, kind and playful find a deeper, steadier kind of closeness.

steps.prompt: Six months in, things feel more routine and less exciting. What’s the healthiest response?

options.text: Plan something new together, and keep asking about each other’s lives.
options.why: Newness and curiosity keep the connection growing past the early buzz.

options.text: Assume the spark is gone and end it.
options.why: A calmer phase is normal, and often where real closeness grows.

options.text: Start looking at dating apps again.
options.why: Looking elsewhere skips the chance to build something deeper.

steps.prompt: Keep it fresh.
steps.why: Doing new things together brings back a bit of that early-days excitement.

steps.prompt: What would you love to grow together in?
steps.reply: Sharing that wish with your partner is a lovely step to take together.

steps.prompt: Match each worry with a way to grow closer.

pairs.b: Try one new thing a month

steps.why: Every phase of a relationship has its own way to grow closer, if you choose it together.

steps.body: Suggest one new experience to try together this month.
